When fused with sparse and noisy observations, the spring--mass ODE acts as a strong inductive bias for downstream tasks: interpolation and parameter estimation. That is, ContinuousCloth reduces interpolation error by 7.3 times over a data-only neural baseline in simulation and 2.4 times on real-world cloth sequences, and achieves 2.6 times lower parameter error than a differentiable-solver baseline under high-noise conditions, demonstrating consistent robustness under realistic measurement imperfections.
item.dc:creator: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Zhuo He, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa

item.title: On the Depth Transfer of Neural Optimizers via L-Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2610.14344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling deep learning models efficiently requires predictable performance transfer across compute regimes. Establishing reliable hyperparameter transfer allows optimal training dynamics and structural choices to be discovered on low-cost proxy models, avoiding catastrophic failures during massive-scale training. Existing depth-transfer analyses are architecture-specific and heuristic: hyperparameter transfer is only justified through toy blocks, and both rely on infinite-depth dynamics, a specific initialization, and feature-learning criteria. Building on $L$-smoothness framework of Xu et al. (2026), we understand hyperparameter transfer as how do the Lipschitz and $L$-smoothness constants of the loss scale with the depth $K$? We show that inverse-depth residual branch scaling $\alpha=\Theta(1/K)$ is sufficient to make both constants depth-independent at fixed width, uniformly over the bounded parameter domain and for arbitrary $p\to q$ geometries. Because the bounds depend on each residual branch only through its Lipschitz and smoothness constants, the argument applies to general residual networks (including branches of block depth $\geq 2$ such as transformer and ResNet blocks) without assumptions on initialization or correlations between layer weights. Since the smoothness constant controls the curvature penalty in the descent inequality, our bounds motivate a learning-rate scale without an additional depth-dependent curvature correction for updates bounded in the prescribed norm. This provides a geometric explanation of inverse-depth residual scaling and its application to the operator-norm geometries associated with AdamW, Muon, and MOGA. Learning-rate sweeps on GPT-2 (depths 2--128) and CIFAR-100 ResNets (8--32 residual blocks) confirm that Muon and MOGA exhibit stable learning-rate transfer under these prescriptions, with a common optimal rate across a 64-fold increase in depth.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Wong, Chenyu Xu, Jiajin Li, Yiping Lu

item.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction for Signal Temporal Logic Inference with Many Classes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) inference provides interpretable formulas for time series classification. For multiclass classification, however, accurate predictions do not necessarily ensure that the inferred formulas are satisfied consistently with the true class. We introduce the positive satisfaction rate and codeword satisfaction rate to quantify satisfaction of required formulas and consistency with the complete class codeword, respectively. We develop a two-stage procedure that first learns discriminative formulas using a margin-based objective and then refines predicate thresholds toward a small positive robustness target while fixing the formula structure and temporal intervals. Satisfaction and ranking penalties discourage violations of required formulas and loss of class separation. The decoding loss is used as a nonconformity score and calibrated separately for each class, providing finite-sample class-conditional coverage under intra-class exchangeability. Experiments on naval, synthetic, and robot manipulation trajectories demonstrate discrepancies between classification accuracy and formula satisfaction. The results further reveal a data-dependent tradeoff between robustness tightness and satisfaction, while class-conditional calibration mitigates undercoverage that can be hidden by pooled calibration.
item.dc:creator: Yixuan Wang, Danyang Li, Matthew Cleaveland, Roberto Tron, Mingyu Cai

item.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
item.description: arXiv:2610.14363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tilde{\Omega}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tilde{\Theta}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.
item.dc:creator: Princewill Okoroafor

item.title: ConformalGuard: False-Positive-Controlled Action Gating for LM Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model classifiers are increasingly deployed for high-stakes decisions such as phishing screening, content moderation, and fraud triage, yet validation-set thresholds provide no finite-sample control of deployment-time false positives. We present ConformalGuard, a model-agnostic calibration layer that wraps a fixed scoring function with finite-sample control over the rate at which legitimate inputs trigger an intervention tier. Our contribution is empirical and operational, not a new conformal theorem: zero-shot LM API scores can be coarse enough (10--11 unique values here) to make temperature scaling and isotonic regression operationally identical to raw thresholding for low-FPR action gating. We compare these methods with conformal calibration for fine-tuned BERT, Claude Sonnet 4, and GPT-4o on public email corpora. For Claude, conformal calibration reduces FPR from 0.040 to 0.008 while recall falls from 0.938 to 0.875. For deterministic GPT-4o scores, the 1% operating point is too conservative to deploy (recall 0.564); three-run stochastic averaging raises recall to 0.732 at FPR 0.005. At 2% prevalence with BERT, conformal calibration removes 25 false-positive reviews per 10,000 emails (95% CI [10, 43]). The guarantee is legitimate-event-rate control under exchangeability; discrimination, workload effects, and robustness to shift remain empirical.
item.dc:creator: Bishnu Bista, Dhanraj Haibatrao Jadhav, Vibha Choudhary, Gaurav Saxena, Arun Pandiyan Perumal, Arjun Subedi, Jignesh Ammineni

item.title: History, Adaptation, and Hidden Gain: Two Prospective Tests of Learned Predictive Control in a Synthetic Neural Population
item.description: arXiv:2610.14368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study learned one-step predictive control of a synthetic population of 64 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons whose light sensitivity is scaled by a hidden factor s, using two prospective confirmations on plants simulated only after the analysis was frozen. In the first (50 plants, 11 conditions), removing the 200-ms input-output history substantially worsened a parameter-count-matched neural predictor at low and moderate gain (s = 0.6, 0.8; RMSE rose by 2.47 Hz at s = 0.6, 97.5% CI 2.43-2.51). In secondary comparisons, recursively adapted ARX had the lowest mean error of the deployable controllers in 10 of 11 conditions, tuned PI with anti-windup matched or beat the network for s >= 0.7, and training for 10,000 rather than 900 epochs lowered prediction error but worsened control. Development work suggested the network's learned action sensitivity did not track the hidden gain. A second protocol (50 new plants, 9 sensitivities, 2 noise levels) confirmed three pre-specified predictions at the primary noise level. Re-estimating a single multiplicative input gain recovered 87% (95% CI 86-88%) of the benefit of full adaptive ARX. Supplying that online estimate to the network as an extra input reduced high-gain tracking error by 1.84 Hz [1.81, 1.88]. Longer training worsened the plain network by 1.09 Hz but improved the gain-input network by 1.07 Hz, a differential of 2.16 Hz [2.13, 2.20]. Under high process noise (sigma = 2.0) the effects shrank to about 0.04 Hz or less and gain-only adaptation recovered only 24% of the adaptive-ARX benefit. In this synthetic plant, at the primary noise level, one-parameter online gain estimation accounts for most of the gap between a history-based network and full adaptive ARX, and for its prediction-control mismatch.
item.dc:creator: Mahesh Reddy Pagadala

item.title: When More Memory Fails: Hidden Feasibility Holes in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization
item.description: arXiv:2610.14369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains neural networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand. A natural expectation is that a budget large enough to complete training stays sufficient when it is increased. Using DTR's reference simulator, simrd, to replay the public DTR training traces, we show that this expectation fails. We call the exceptions feasibility holes: memory budgets at which an eviction policy runs out of memory although both a smaller and a larger budget complete, a form of non-monotone feasibility. Under a written sweep protocol with dated amendments, a 0.01-step budget grid shows no such hole for DTR on any of six confirmatory traces, although unresolved timeouts prevent it from establishing monotonicity. Finer sampling finds holes on InceptionV4 (three regions) and U-Net (two regions), in addition to one on the ResNet-32 development trace. Every hole is reproduced by three repeats and by unmodified simrd. For one InceptionV4 pair (0.2343 versus 0.235 of peak memory) we trace the failure to individual allocations. The larger budget avoids one eviction at an operator where the smaller budget was 173,479 bytes short. The extra data it carries forward forces a later eviction of a tensor needed three operators afterwards, and rebuilding that tensor triggers a recomputation cascade that cannot fit. Keeping that one tensor resident under the same budget prevents the failure. The two simple score changes we tested do not remove holes across traces; both add failing budgets on some traces. All results are from simulation, with no allocator model; behaviour on GPU hardware is untested.
item.dc:creator: Mahesh Reddy Pagadala

item.title: DPAL: A Test-Time Adaptation Loss for Financial Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.14376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables time series forecasters to update after deployment as new observations become available. However, adaptation objectives that focus primarily on prediction errors at individual time steps do not fully address the needs of financial time series forecasting. In addition to pointwise return fitting, return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns are also important. To better account for these properties, we introduce Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (DPAL), which combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms. We apply DPAL within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without modifying the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings.
item.dc:creator: Wuzhou Lian, Haochun Wang, Yuefan Deng

item.title: Clinical value claims in multimodal AI outpace supporting evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.14395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal prediction models add a data source, such as imaging or an assay, to clinical information, and health systems must decide whether that added test is worth acquiring. We audited 177 studies comparing multimodal with unimodal models: 81 from a systematic review and 96 from a probability sample of 2025-2026 PubMed records. Gains in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were smaller when a study fitted a separate model for every data source (adjusted difference, -0.030; 95% CI, -0.056 to -0.005). Within 78 such studies, leaving out the strongest source's model would have raised the average gain from 0.046 to 0.108. This complete benchmarking fell from 69.1% of review studies to an estimated 46.0% of recent ones. An estimated 22% assessed decision utility and none evaluated a model prospectively, yet most claimed potential clinical usefulness or improved care (84.0% and an estimated 87.7%).
item.dc:creator: Jiayu Feng

item.title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
item.dc:creator: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du

item.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
item.dc:creator: Alex Gower

item.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
item.dc:creator: Shihua Yu, Yanzhi Wang, Tianchi Chen

item.title: Design Choices for Multimodal Transformer Learning with Missing and Longitudinal Healthcare Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.14436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal learning offers the potential to improve predictions by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous data sources. However, multimodal datasets are frequently incomplete, raising important questions about how models should handle missing information. Although recent approaches increasingly rely on Transformer-based architectures for multimodal fusion, incomplete multimodal data introduces challenges such as missing modalities and intra-modal missingness, which motivate key architectural design choices, such as tokenization granularity. In addition, many datasets are longitudinal, with observations collected across multiple time points. The sequential nature of the Transformer architectures provides a natural framework for modeling such data, but introduces additional considerations, such as how temporal information should be represented. In this study, we systematically investigate these design choices using three different cancer datasets. We compare modality-level and feature-level tokenization and evaluate attention masking and imputation as strategies for handling missing information, both naturally occurring in the datasets and synthetically induced. We further investigate approaches for incorporating temporal information in our training process and how to model it. Experiments are conducted with unimodal and multimodal configurations, as well as different levels of missingness for binary survival classification and multiple time encoding strategies for discrete-time survival prediction. Our results show that while multimodal outperforms unimodal results, missing data heavily impacts predictions and thus effective design choices such as tokenization granularity, and intra-missing handling is essential for reliable prediction.
item.dc:creator: Rita Cordeiro Mendes, Maria Manuel Pereira, Carlos Santiago, Catarina Barata

item.title: From Transfer Probes to Expert Grouping: Evidence from LoRA Post-Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.14437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A platform that post-trains one base model for many business lines often has more lines than experts it can maintain, so lines must share experts, yet lines seldom come with a taxonomy saying which should share. We ask whether transfer probes (train on one source, measure paired changes on all sources) can discover a grouping when the standard one is unknown. To test probes against a reference, we use seven public sources that do have a label tree (five mathematics subfields and two kinds of programming, standing in for business lines) and treat the tree's grouping as a label reference that the evaluator holds and the method does not. With four LoRA experts under fixed per-source exposure and per-expert budgets, we compare a purely probe-derived grouping and an uninformed uniform default (whose tied routing serves every line from one expert) against this reference. Trained once for one interval from a shared warm-up state and routed by a rule fixed by each allocation, neither reached the prespecified practical gain of 2 percentage points, and both had lower overall utility than the reference ($-2.43$ and $-2.54$ pp; 95\% intervals below zero). In a post hoc comparison, the probe-derived grouping was indistinguishable from the uniform default ($+0.11$ pp, $[-1.25,+1.54]$). In fixed-budget LoRA post-training, a grouping built from initial-state single-source probes thus did not deliver the advantage predicted from the probes once carried to a later training state, a finite budget, and specified routing.
item.dc:creator: Xueyang Wu

item.title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.14440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $\rho$ by $\rho^\alpha$ for a data-adaptive exponent $\alpha\in[0,1]$: $\alpha=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $\alpha=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $\alpha$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $\kappa$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$\alpha$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.
item.dc:creator: Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Kayhan Behdin, Wenhui Zhu, Aida Rahmattalabi, Jincheng Cao, Jelena Markovic-Voronov, Alborz Geramifard

item.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2610.14448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
item.dc:creator: Sihwan Park, Sung-Yub Kim, Doohyuk Jang, Eunho Yang

item.title: Learning to Extrapolate in Depth with Looped Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped transformers reuse a single block across iterations, raising a natural question: how far can a block trained at one depth be safely extrapolated to greater depths? We study this question for all-pairs graph connectivity, where harder graphs require longer-range information propagation. We show that under exchangeability and symmetric positive initialization, population training at depth K converges to an update rule governed by a single effective parameter that balances graph propagation against fitting structure unresolved at training depth. This trade-off creates a finite extrapolation window: too few test-time loops provide insufficient propagation, while too many eventually create false connections. We derive explicit endpoints for this window and bound the graph hardness solvable beyond training as a function of training depth and hardness. In particular, a test depth chosen solely from the training distribution can guarantee recovery on substantially harder graphs, with a certified depth gain that grows exponentially as training depth outpaces training hardness. Experiments validate the predicted windows and show how compute budget and initialization affect the optimal training depth.
item.dc:creator: Huitao Yang, Jianhao Huang, Zixuan Wang, Baharan Mirzasoleiman

item.title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.
item.dc:creator: Cong Wang, Jin Li, Shoujin Wang, Yishuo Li, Huilin Gu, Wenpeng Lu

item.title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.
item.dc:creator: M Jawad, HV Gupta, MA Farmani, A Behrangi, GY Niu

item.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.
item.dc:creator: Yuqiu Deng, Muyun Jiang, Zongpeng Zhang, Mingqing Xiao, Yansen Wang, Peiliang Gong, Xinliang Zhou, Yi Ding, Ziyu Jia, Cuntai Guan, Chenyu Liu

item.title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.
item.dc:creator: Zirui Peng, Heyi Zheng, Ziming Liu

item.title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
item.dc:creator: Yanxi Pan, Jingwen Wu, Yan Ma, Xiang Chen, Xinyi Zeng, Xuetong Wang, Yunyan Zhang, Yue Zhang, Yu Tian, Jianfeng Pan, Hongyi Zhou

item.title: Active Neural Matter: A Finite-Window Response Framework for Physical Systems and Distributed AI Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.14549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical systems and distributed AI workflows can retain past information, receive delayed feedback and combine conflicting signals. These features pose a common modeling problem: determining what information about past interactions a state must retain to account for future responses. Active Neural Matter (ANM) addresses this problem through a finite-window response framework. Forward analysis uses each system's dynamics to predict state and output responses to perturbations, separating propagation from output sensitivity. Inverse analysis tests whether a candidate state retains enough information for these responses. With the system and future inputs or interaction rules fixed, distinguishable responses from histories assigned the same state identify distinctions the representation must preserve. Their distributional separation gives a lower bound on the worst-case error of approximating behavior from that state. Uncertainty bounds distinguish rejection, support within a fixed tolerance on tested comparisons, and unresolved cases. Delayed-consensus simulations check analytical predictions of response amplitude and phase over a narrow range of delays; flocking illustrates dependence on the chosen observable. An exact delayed-return construction establishes a sufficient state for a specified program. The AI studies identify distinctions in interaction history and evidence order that a representation must preserve to reproduce observed response distributions. Tests on new histories in a controlled feedback task provide bounded support for a state specified by the task instructions; the instructed rule predicts every observed action. ANM connects response prediction to measurable information requirements, separating behavioral fidelity from task correctness and initial-state adequacy from a closed evolution law for that state.
item.dc:creator: Tianchi Chen, Shihua Yu

item.title: PGSB: Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis for LoRA Model Merging
item.description: arXiv:2610.14558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large pretrained models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet adapting them to multiple downstream tasks remains challenging: full fine-tuning is costly, while maintaining separate task-specific models is storage-inefficient and fails to produce a unified multi-task model. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers an efficient alternative for Model Merging by representing each task adaptation as a low-rank update over frozen pretrained weights. However, existing LoRA merging methods often treat task-specific updates as directly comparable objects and merge them in their original low-rank parameter spaces. This overlooks two key factors: which update directions provide reliable shared support across tasks, and how these directions should be re-parameterized with respect to the pretrained weights before merging. To address this limitation, we propose Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis (PGSB), a two-stage framework for LoRA model merging. PGSB first identifies shared directions among task-specific LoRA updates, and then re-parameterizes these directions using their interaction with the pretrained weights, producing a more suitable basis for merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PGSB consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/Kitschnada/Pretrained-Basis .
item.dc:creator: Muqing Liu, Chongjie Si, Zhuoya Liu, Yuheng Jia

item.title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69\% and 58.67\% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yilan Chen, Zian Su, Manish Prajapat, Dingmin Wang, Rein Houthooft, Rui Song, Vijay Lingam

item.title: LLM-Augmented Bayesian Optimization with Adaptive Policies for Chiplet Design Space Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2610.14612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiplet technology is a key approach for extending Moore's Law. However, its design process is constrained by two primary challenges: the scarcity of early-stage platforms for rapidly evaluating chiplet-based heterogeneous systems, and the complex relationships between design parameters and optimization metrics. To address these challenges, we propose a synergistic framework that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) with Bayesian Optimization (BO), enabling architectural-level simulation and automated optimization for the 2.5D/3D CPU-GPU heterogeneous chiplets. We extend the open-source chiplet simulator to evaluate 3D designs by supporting graph topologies. Further, to enhance the exploration efficiency of BO, we introduce an LLM that generates high-quality policies to guide the optimization process, enabled by our proposed adaptive directional policy reasoning (ADPR) and an exploration gain-aware fine-tuning method. Finally, we use the policy-guided BO to perform an automated and efficient exploration of the complex chiplet design space. Experiments on 2.5D and 3D chiplet reveal that our framework improves design space exploration efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Hang Liu, Zhengfei Chen, Zhengrui Chen, Hao Geng, Yu Li, Qi Sun

item.title: From Rainfall to Road-Network Functionality: Transferable Graph Forecasting for Flood-Disrupted Transportation Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.14622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extreme rainfall can rapidly degrade road-network functionality (RNF), disrupting emergency mobility, accessibility, evacuation, logistics, and infrastructure restoration. Existing flood-transportation impact models are often difficult to deploy across regions because they rely on local calibration, intensive simulation workflows or target-region retraining. This study proposes G-R2R, a transferable spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that reframes rainfall-induced road-network disruption as a region-conditioned, topology-flexible graph forecasting problem for unseen transportation networks. The framework integrates ego-centered subgraph sampling, terrain-conditioned graph representation, region-conditioned dual-level static encoding, and dynamic rainfall-network feature learning. Static geographic and infrastructure attributes are fused with rainfall forcing and recent RNF states to forecast node-level RNF across heterogeneous road networks. G-R2R is evaluated using simulation-derived RNF sequences from ten flood-prone regions in Wenzhou, China, under unseen-region testing protocols. It outperforms representative forecasting baselines, achieving a stabilized MAPE of 2.33% and $R^2$ of 0.855 under the fixed unseen-region benchmark. Leave-one-area-out evaluation yields stabilized MAPE values of 2.30%-3.54%. Ablation analysis supports the contributions of the terrain-conditioned graph representation and dual-level static encoding. A historical-event replay of Typhoon Fitow further shows that G-R2R reproduces principal temporal trajectories and node-level spatial patterns of the simulation-derived RNF reference under observed rainfall forcing without target-region retraining. These results support rapid and transferable node-level RNF forecasting across the regional road-network domains represented in this study.
item.dc:creator: Junyan Wang, Naiyu Wang

item.title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.14626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. In scientific optimization, this assumption is often violated, leading to surrogate representations that are poorly aligned with the optimization objective. To address this limitation, we propose TagBO (Task-aware Graph Bayesian Optimization), a method that integrates LLM-derived relational priors with descriptor-based struc?tural information for mixed-variable Bayesian optimization. Rather than directly using LLM outputs as predictive scores, TagBO treats LLM outputs as a potentially noisy source of task-aware relational priors and extracts coarse ordinal relational signals from LLM reasoning to construct task-aware similarity structures for scien?tific optimization. TagBO then performs constrained Gaussian process Bayesian optimization over the resulting joint discrete-continuous representation space. Ex?periments on diverse chemistry and materials formulation tasks demonstrate that TagBO consistently improves sample efficiency under fixed evaluation budgets across LLMs of varying capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Xinzhe Yuan, Zimu Zeng, Zhuo Chen, Jianshu Zhang, Jinzong Dong, Jingyi Chen, Nanyang Ye, Huan Xiong, Qinying Gu

item.title: Ascent Conditions for Length-Normalized Single-Rollout Policy Updates
item.description: arXiv:2610.14670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dividing each trajectory's score contribution by its realized length can change the direction of a reward-centered policy update. In a finite trajectory model, we derive an exact ascent threshold for a three-outcome softmax policy and exhibit a binary-reward example in which the expected Euclidean update decreases task success. Natural-gradient ascent holds for fully controllable outcome distributions with deterministic binary labels, but can fail under a one-parameter restriction. A third-order U-statistic estimates the first-order return change without bias from independent current-policy trajectories, one per request. In the example, a same-sample plug-in estimator instead has the opposite sign in expectation for batch sizes two through forty-nine. Exact policy-grid enumeration confirms the local sign reversal. In a branching process, length-normalized learning initially loses return, then recovers and exceeds the unnormalized comparator. The analysis concerns the expected update field at the current policy.
item.dc:creator: Levin David Schwab

item.title: Triage-PiEvo: Evidence Admission for Principle-Evolving Scientific Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based AI Scientists advance scientific discovery, yet they suffer from inefficiencies due to noisy observations. Existing principle-evolving agents act on every anomaly, leaving its source unresolved: a new mechanism or an evaluation artifact, so invalid revisions bias evolution. To address this, we formulate revision as evidence admission: anomalies steer search immediately, but only independently verified evidence may rewrite persistent principles, and contradicted principles are retracted. We realize this in TRIAGE-PIEVO , which pairs an anomaly-responsive search portfolio with a staged verification gate that alone controls what enters principle state. Across four scientific tasks with three backbones, TRIAGE-PIEVO (1) attains the highest average solution quality with +7.5%~11.8% over the strongest baseline per backbone, matching the strongest baseline's full-budget quality with one-third of the evaluation budget on Qwen3-235B; and additional stress tests and cross-harness deployment demonstrate that (2) in constructed stress tests, it admits none of the corrupted, hidden-source, or exploit evidence that ungated variants admit, while missing no planted mechanism, and (3) plugged unchanged into three external research harnesses, it cuts false evidence admissions by over 60% and raises verified scores by 31%~43%.
item.dc:creator: Peize Li, Yingming Pu, Xingguo Xu, Yiming Cui, Yuansheng Gao, Tao Lin

item.title: One-Way Coupling via Patchwise Adaptive Normalization in Transformer Surrogates
item.description: arXiv:2610.14687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many physical systems exhibit one-way coupling: exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry influence the dynamics without being affected by them. We investigate how explicitly representing these fields can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based PDE surrogates. Building on spatially adaptive normalization, we introduce Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (PAdaNorm), which partitions exogenous fields into patches aligned with the state tokenization. We evaluate PAdaNorm on datasets from three different domains, using a Walrus-inspired transformer architecture. Across the three PDE families, PAdaNorm is on par with or up to 16% better than parameter-matched baselines in mean long-horizon variance-scaled RMSE on 60-step autoregressive rollouts. We also find that PAdaNorm better maintains hard physical constraints over long rollouts, such as preventing flow into impenetrable solid regions in porous media. When the conditioning is static, PAdaNorm caches the conditioning embeddings once and reuses them across the entire rollout, reducing inference FLOPs per step by up to 36% compared with parameter-matched baselines. An ablation over eight conditioning variants shows that modulating a single attention axis (temporal or spatial) suffices and that a lightweight shared MLP across blocks remains competitive with per-block projections.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Gottlob, Hugo Thimonier, Ludovico Buizza, August Martens, Alexandre Gavaudan, Thiago Guzella

item.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
item.description: arXiv:2610.14688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: SIGMOD 2027
item.dc:creator: Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao

item.title: Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.14696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.
item.dc:creator: Maria B{\aa}nkestad, Jens Sj\"olund

item.title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
item.description: arXiv:2610.14703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"{\i}ve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"{\i}ve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Spallanzani

item.title: DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.14710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Peiyuan Li, Yongqi Huang, Jitao Zhao, Di Jin, Dongxiao He

item.title: Multi-Token Random-Walk Learning via Meeting-Triggered Information Exchange
item.description: arXiv:2610.14716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random walk (RW)-based algorithms are widely used in decentralized learning due to their low communication overhead and scalability. While most existing methods rely on a single token, multiple tokens can explore the network in parallel and exchange information upon meeting. However, the fundamental benefits of such meeting-triggered interactions remain unclear. In this work, we investigate multi-token RW learning under two information exchange policies: \textsc{Average-Gradient} and \textsc{Average-Model}, which average stochastic gradients and updated models, respectively, when tokens meet. We establish iteration complexity lower bounds for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives on complete graphs, which apply to both exchange policies. Compared with single-token RW learning, the scaling factor in these bounds is reduced by a factor of $m^2$ for non-convex and convex objectives, and by an exponentially in $m$ for strongly convex objectives, where $m$ denotes the number of tokens. Numerical experiments reveal distinct behaviors of the two policies under two performance criteria: mean-token loss (the average loss across all tokens) and best-token loss (the minimum loss across all tokens). \textsc{Average-Model} achieves lower mean-token loss and is relatively insensitive to the network-to-token ratio $N/m$, where $N$ is the number of nodes. In contrast, \textsc{Average-Gradient} achieves lower best-token loss but exhibits a trade-off between parallel exploration and gradient interference as $N/m$ decreases.
item.dc:creator: Taichun Yeh, Xingran Chen

item.title: Integrating AIRL-Based Reward Estimation into a Control Method Using Fuzzy Inference and Policy Gradient
item.description: arXiv:2610.14723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A method integrating policy gradient with fuzzy inference has been proposed. This method, hereafter referred to as the base model, has high flexibility with respect to the configuration of fuzzy inference rules and fuzzy representation. It can also automatically adjust the rule weights and the membership functions in the antecedent and consequent parts using the same framework for learning. In methods that integrate reinforcement learning with fuzzy inference, however, the reward function must be designed in advance. It is therefore useful to add learning-based reward estimation to the base model. This paper proposes a fuzzy control method that integrates a reward estimation mechanism based on the adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) framework into the base model. The generative adversarial nets (GAN) framework adopted in AIRL, however, tends to suffer from unstable learning. To address this, the proposed method treats the policy of the base model as the generator and also uses the set of membership functions in the policy as the cost function of the discriminator. This configuration allows the discriminator update for reward estimation and the generator update for policy estimation to be performed simultaneously on the parameters shared by both, without estimating a value function. In simulations of an illustrative vehicle speed control task, the proposed method acquired policies with high generalization performance through stable and efficient learning.
item.dc:creator: Seiji Ishihara

item.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2610.14731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
item.dc:creator: Muquan Yu, Dihan Hu

item.title: PTGPO: Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.14737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is challenging because sparse terminal rewards provide weak credit signals for intermediate actions. Existing group-based methods either assign a shared trajectory-level advantage or estimate step-level advantages from state groups, which may conflate the current action with subsequent decisions. We propose Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (PTGPO), a critic-free method that constructs prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within anchor-state groups. PTGPO assigns each tree edge a credit given by the difference between its child and parent empirical mean returns, capturing the conditional return change revealed by each additional action. These prefix-tree credits provide fine-grained learning signals without requiring a critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on interactive benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban show that PTGPO consistently improves over RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Ruolin Chen, Yang Li, Jihang Wang, Zhuoya Zhao, Yuchen Liu, Jiaming Xu, Qian Zhang

item.title: More Domains, No Gains? FLO: Fast-Slow Reciprocal Learning for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
item.description: arXiv:2610.14748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by the great success of foundation models in the development of artificial general intelligence, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently attracted significant attention and have the potential to advance graph intelligence. Exhibiting such intelligence requires effectively learning knowledge from large-scale, multi-domain graph data during pre-training. Increasing domain diversity during pre-training is expected to yield richer and more generalizable knowledge. Most existing methods pursue this goal by designing domain alignment strategies that help a single graph model learn from multiple domains. However, we observe that existing methods struggle to benefit from increasing domain diversity. Through empirical and theoretical analysis, we reveal two key limitations. Firstly, pre-training in most GFMs is confined to a single message-passing paradigm. Since propagation flattens relations among neighboring nodes, the graph model can hardly perceive the knowledge beyond propagation, namely the attribute-predictable component of these relations. Secondly, domain alignment strategies often rely on randomly initialized parameters that are jointly updated with the graph model using immediate loss feedback, leaving early knowledge acquisition vulnerable to cross-domain interference. To address these issues, we propose FLO, a Fast--sLow reciprOcal approach for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, a propagation-free attribute branch predicts the graph model's relations without message passing and returns these predictions to refine the model. We further stabilize knowledge acquisition by pairing a fast process that adapts to the current domain with a slow process that integrates knowledge across domains. On 12 datasets, FLO benefits from increasing domain diversity and achieves the best average performance in cross-domain and cross-task transfer.
item.dc:creator: Yupeng Tong, Lianze Shan, Jitao Zhao, Di Jin, Dongxiao He

item.title: Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.14751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarl\'{o}s and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.
item.dc:creator: Sepideh Mahabadi, Sandeep Silwal, Tal Wagner

item.title: CrossMean: Model Merging by Pairing Merged and Expert Activations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one network without retraining, and closed-form methods compute each merged layer from statistics of its input activations. However, these statistics are measured on a single expert, while in the merged model, each layer receives activations from the merged layers that precede it. Recent work re-measures these statistics in the merged model but still forms them from a single network. We formulate closed-form methods as a linear system and show that they use the same matrix on both sides. We then introduce CrossMean, which replaces this matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. From the same statistics, we also derive a label-free criterion that indicates the task sets in which accounting for the merged activations improves the merge more. Empirically, task sets with a lower criterion value show a larger improvement. On the eight-task benchmark of each vision backbone that we tested and on BERT encoders, CrossMean improves on merging with statistics measured on the experts, and with all linear layers merged, it also improves on re-measuring these statistics in the merged model. These results suggest that merging benefits from pairing merged and expert activations.
item.dc:creator: Moshe Eliasof

item.title: Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.
item.dc:creator: Tillmann Rheude, Roland Eils, Benjamin Wild

item.title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.
item.dc:creator: Renjie Cao, Yifei Cheng, Li Shen

item.title: Groups Don't Move as One: A Bregman Clustering View of Linearized Group Influence
item.description: arXiv:2610.14809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Influence functions provide an efficient alternative to retraining for assessing the effects of removing or reweighting training data. For groups, however, the standard first-order estimate reduces individual contributions to a sum that can conceal substantial differences among members, including opposing effects that cancel. We establish a Bregman centroid formulation of the linearized group influence objective, interpreting this aggregate as a single representative and using Bregman information (BI) to quantify the variation it omits. Extending this formulation to multiple clusters reveals distinct contributions whose sum recovers the original estimate. We further propose an estimator that jointly optimizes the weights of these cluster contributions, rather than simply summing them. Experiments uncover cluster-specific influence patterns and a positive association between target-specific BI and approximation error. The proposed estimator achieves higher $R^2$ than standard group influence in predicting target changes under the nonlinear proximal Bregman response function. Simplified clustering and correction variants reduce computational cost. The centroid view thus explains what additive group influence leaves out and provides a basis for using that information to improve estimation.
item.dc:creator: Hyunho Choi, Jaeseung Heo, Youngbin Choi, MoonJeong Park, Dongwoo Kim

item.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.
item.dc:creator: Neesha Naimeen, Victor Miranda Soberanis

item.title: Sequence-Structured Decision Learning for Branch-and-Bound in Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
item.description: arXiv:2610.14835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Branch-and-bound (BnB) solves mixed-integer linear programs by constructing and exploring a search tree. Node selection and branching are two recurrent decisions that directly determine the tree. Learning-based approaches typically optimize either decision in isolation and condition on a mostly local view, leaving the coupled evolution of the search tree insufficiently modeled. This paper proposes Seq-BnB, a sequence-structured framework that learns branching and node selection from a shared global representation of the evolving BnB process. Seq-BnB serializes node creations, node updates, node-selection events, and branching events into typed tokens, producing a causal event sequence of the search trajectory. A self-attention encoder summarizes this global search history, a bipartite graph neural network encodes the current LP relaxation, and context-conditioned decision heads score branching variables and open nodes. To reduce distribution shift between expert demonstrations and learned policies, Seq-BnB is trained with DAgger-style data aggregation. On four MILP benchmark families, Seq-BnB consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines, with strong solution times on both standard and larger transfer instances. While this paper evaluates Seq-BnB instantiation for branching and node selection, it accommodates additional solver decisions, such as cut selection, by introducing new action tokens and decision heads.
item.dc:creator: Tengfei Liu, Jinrun Liu, Bai Yan, Yuhui Shi, Qi Zhao

item.title: Disentangling Marginal Capacity from Geometry in Optimal-Transport Label Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2610.14853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal transport (OT) is widely used to align distributions and transfer labels between unpaired source and target data, but source-target composition shifts can cause rare classes to be systematically under-predicted even with high transport confidence. We identify a source of this failure in the transport marginal: under the standard uniform weighting of source points, each class has transport capacity proportional to its source frequency, which can be insufficient to meet its target demand even when separated well in the embedding space. We show that displaced mass is preferentially absorbed by high-capacity classes rather than geometrically similar classes, producing confident errors that are difficult to detect from the transport plan. Downstream read-outs, entropic smoothing, and marginal relaxation provide limited recovery, whereas matching the transport marginal to the target composition substantially improves label transfer. On single-cell data, the oracle composition-matched marginal raises macro-F1 from 0.322 to 0.623, and the best deployable estimator closes 69% of the oracle gap. Correcting the marginal also separates a coverage-dependent component of error from residual error associated with class separability, showing that transport capacity and representation geometry are distinct sources of transfer error.
item.dc:creator: Ali Khodabandeh Yalabadi, Azim Dehghani Amirabad, Artem Moskalev, Yun-Ching Chen, Mehdi Pirooznia, Scott Oloff, Rui Liao

item.title: Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds
item.description: arXiv:2610.14860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought the vision of a general-purpose personal assistant closer to reality. Such assistants could provide a unified natural-language interface to a broad ecosystem of applications. However, real-world applications do not readily support training at scale because access is often restricted and their state is difficult to reset. To address this challenge, we introduce Terrarium, a framework that synthesizes executable App Worlds from real-world application information, generates training task packages with evaluator-side rubrics from these worlds, and iteratively validates and refines both through agent rollouts. For App World synthesis, Terrarium organizes public Web information and in-application observations into structured app specifications that guide the construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state.
