We introduce ECLIPTICA, which treats alignment as instruction-driven and runtime-controllable: natural-language alignment instructions act as an explicit behavioral contract (stance, refusal boundary, verbosity) that modulates behavior on the fly under evolving safety requirements, user roles, and governance constraints. We introduce CITA (Contrastive Instruction-Tuned Alignment), combining SFT with contrastive preference optimization under an explicit geometric anchor to a reference model. This yields a stable Riemannian chart and keeps instruction updates within a shared neighborhood, so regimes stay nearby and traversable for reliable switching. To isolate policy switching from ordinary instruction following, we release the ECLIPTICA benchmark: 3000 controlled cases (300 prompts x 10 instruction types) where the user request is fixed and only the alignment instruction changes. On Llama-3.1-8B across five suites (ECLIPTICA, TruthfulQA, Conditional Safety, Length Control, LITMUS), CITA reaches 86.7% instruction-alignment efficiency, beating DPO (56.1%), GRPO (36.1%), and PPO (20.4%).
item.dc:creator: Kapil Wanaskar, Gaytri Jena, Vinija Jain, Aman Chadha, Amitava Das

item.title: Architecture Before the Formula: Training-Dependent Computational Semantics in Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2601.11618v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An operation's input-output function does not, by itself, determine its computational role within a represented process. That role also depends on the processes producing its inputs and receiving its outputs, a philosophical stance termed deep learning externalism (DLE). We develop a mathematical account of represented computation that distinguishes functional equivalence, retained predecessor distinctions, restricted receiver capability, and context-dependent effective architectures. The resulting equivalences depend on which computational relations a scientific description must preserve. We prove that two injective producer contexts can preserve every predecessor distinction while changing whether fixed local and attention receiver families are equivalent. We investigate these relations in a dimension-labelled PreNorm Transformer and their evolution under training. Residual bypasses restrict complete-state information identifications to two merges per block, while finer branches can change receiver accessibility. Exact gradient-descent models yield covariance-dependent geometric attenuation under learned producer routing and algebraic $(t^{-1/2})$ attenuation under Q/K-softmax training, with optimal bounded-receiver recovery errors derived in both cases. Coupled producer-attention dynamics establish how learning jointly reorganizes the presented features and receiver allocation. Finally, present functional or receiver-profile equivalence need not determine future behavior under an optimizer. In an input-conditioned attention model, two accessibility measurements form an exact reduced predictive state, whereas one alone does not.
item.dc:creator: Luis F. Rosario Freytes

item.title: Unrolled Neural Networks for Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2601.17274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop unrolled neural networks to solve constrained optimization problems, offering accelerated, learnable counterparts to dual ascent (DA) algorithms. Our framework, termed constrained dual unrolling (CDU), comprises two coupled neural networks that jointly approximate the saddle point of the Lagrangian. The primal network emulates an iterative optimizer that finds a stationary point of the Lagrangian for a given dual multiplier, sampled from an unknown distribution. The dual network generates trajectories towards the optimal multipliers across its layers while querying the primal network at each layer. Unlike standard unrolling, which maps the updates of a prescribed iterative solver directly to network layers, CDU preserves the underlying optimization dynamics while learning the update mappings. The desired primal-dual dynamics are therefore induced through constrained learning by enforcing primal-descent and dual-ascent constraints. We formulate training the two networks as a nested optimization problem and propose an alternating procedure that updates the primal and dual networks in turn, mitigating uncertainty in the multiplier distribution required for primal network training. We establish theoretical guarantees on the feasibility and optimality of the coupled networks. We numerically evaluate the framework on quadratic programs (QPs) with linear constraints and power allocation in wireless networks.
item.dc:creator: Samar Hadou, Alejandro Ribeiro

item.title: Signal from Structure: Exploiting Submodular Upper Bounds in Generative Flow Networks
item.description: arXiv:2601.21061v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; GFNs) are a class of generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their a priori unknown value, their reward. We focus on the case where the reward has a specified, actionable structure, namely that it is submodular. We show submodularity can be harnessed to retrieve upper bounds on the reward of compositional objects that have not yet been observed. We provide in-depth analyses of the probability of such bounds occurring, as well as how many unobserved compositional objects can be covered by a bound. Following the Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty principle, we then introduce SUBo-GFN , which uses the submodular upper bounds to train a GFN. We show that SUBo-GFN generates orders of magnitude more learning signal than classical GFNs for the same number of queries to the reward function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SUBo-GFN in terms of distribution matching and high-quality candidate generation on graph submodular tasks.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Larouche, Audrey Durand

item.title: Scalable Power Sampling: Unlocking Efficient, Training-Free Reasoning for LLMs via Distribution Sharpening
item.description: arXiv:2601.21590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is a dominant approach for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), yet growing evidence suggests that its gains arise primarily from distribution sharpening rather than the acquisition of new capabilities. Recent work has shown that sampling from the power distribution of LLMs using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) can recover performance comparable to RL post-training without relying on external rewards; however, the high computational cost of MCMC makes such approaches impractical for widespread adoption. In this work, we propose a theoretically grounded alternative that eliminates the need for iterative MCMC. We derive a token-level decomposition of the autoregressive power distribution, showing that the global power distribution can be approximated by a token-level scaled low-temperature one, where the scaling factor captures future trajectory quality. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a training-free and verifier-free algorithm that sharpens the base model's generative distribution autoregressively. Empirically, we evaluate our method on math, QA, and code tasks, and show that our method matches or surpasses one-shot GRPO without relying on any external rewards, while reducing inference latency by over $10\times$ compared to MCMC-based sampling.
item.dc:creator: Xiaotong Ji, Rasul Tutunov, Matthieu Zimmer, Haitham Bou Ammar

item.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Spectral Structures in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
item.description: arXiv:2601.21731v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) perform approximate Bayesian inference in a single forward pass, and tabular foundation models (TFMs) built on them are now widely used. To understand what networks infer internally, recent mechanistic studies of TFMs locate where predictions form, but treat these models as tabular predictors rather than as PFNs. It therefore remains unknown whether PFNs represent the spectral content of their context, the quantity that specifies a stationary kernel, and whether this content can be read out as an explicit kernel. We answer both questions. First, across seven PFNs, including four pretrained TFMs and a model trained only on a decision-tree prior, a linear probe on the residual stream recovers the frequency of the context with $R^2 \geq 0.95$. This structure is led by a single principal direction. Second, activation and subspace patching show that the network uses the structure through a low-dimensional subspace, where a few spectral directions move predictions far more than random ones. This holds even for the decision-tree model, so a spectral training prior is not required. On real datasets with up to 499 features, 64 of the 192 directions of TabPFN, chosen without labels, carry 85 to 95\% of the causal effect of the context in all but one pair. Third, we introduce a Filter Bank Decoder that turns frozen PFN representations into an explicit stationary kernel through Bochner's theorem. Without any test-time optimization, the decoded kernel supports Gaussian process regression competitive with deep kernel learning and random Fourier features at about $200\times$ lower cost. PFN latents therefore hold spectral structure that is causally used and recoverable as a portable kernel.
item.dc:creator: Kaustubh Sharma, Srijan Tiwari, Ojasva Nema, Parikshit Pareek

item.title: Transfer Denoising of Low-Rank Plus Sparse Matrices under Ambient and Rank Growth
item.description: arXiv:2601.21873v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study transfer learning for low-rank plus sparse matrix denoising when both ambient and latent dimensions grow. A data-rich source task provides subspace information for a higher-dimensional, data-scarce target with a small rank increment and localized sparse edits. We develop an anchored alternating-projection estimator that preserves transferred subspaces while learning target-specific coefficients, additional latent directions, and sparse modifications. We establish deterministic error bounds that separate target noise, representation growth, and source-estimation error, identifying improved rates through small structural increments and reduced noise within inherited subspaces. We further extend it to approximate anchoring quantifies robustness to subspace mismatch. We establish application-specific guarantees for Markov transition matrix estimation from single trajectories with dependent noise and for structured covariance estimation, with the latter analysis provided in the appendix. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over non-transfer baselines on synthetic data and an approximately 45\% reduction in principal-angle error on a NYC taxi transition-estimation task with expanding state spaces.
item.dc:creator: Elynn Chen, Jinhang Chai, Xuyuan Liu, Yujun Yan

item.title: Federate the Router: Learning Language Model Routers with Sparse and Decentralized Evaluations
item.description: arXiv:2601.22318v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessed as remotely hosted services by edge and enterprise clients that cannot run frontier models locally. Since models vary widely in capability and price, routing queries to models that balance quality and inference cost is essential. Existing router approaches assume access to centralized query-model evaluation data. However, these data are often fragmented across clients, such as end users and organizations, and are privacy-sensitive, which makes centralizing data infeasible. Additionally, per-client router training is ineffective since local evaluation data is limited and covers only a restricted query distribution and a biased subset of model evaluations. We introduce the first federated framework for LLM routing, enabling clients to learn a shared routing policy from local offline query-model evaluation data. Our framework supports both parametric multilayer perceptron router and nonparametric K-means router under heterogeneous client query distributions and non-uniform model coverage. Across three benchmarks, federated collaboration improves the accuracy-cost frontier over client-local routers, both via increased effective model coverage and better query generalization. Our theoretical results also validate that federated training reduces routing suboptimality.
item.dc:creator: Baris Askin, Shivam Patel, Anupam Nayak, Andrea Vigano, Jiin Woo, Gauri Joshi, Carlee Joe-Wong

item.title: FIRE: Multi-fidelity Regression with Distribution-conditioned In-context Learning using Tabular Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.22371v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-fidelity (MF) regression often operates in regimes of extreme data imbalance, where the commonly-used Gaussian-process (GP) surrogates struggle with cubic scaling costs and overfit to sparse high-fidelity observations, limiting efficiency and generalization in real-world applications. We introduce FIRE, a training-free MF framework that couples tabular foundation models (TFMs) to perform zero-shot in-context Bayesian inference via a high-fidelity correction model conditioned on the low-fidelity model's posterior predictive distributions. This cross-fidelity information transfer via distributional summaries captures heteroscedastic errors, enabling robust residual learning without model retraining. Across 31 benchmark problems spanning synthetic and real-world tasks (e.g., DrivAerNet, LCBench), FIRE delivers a stronger performance-time trade-off than seven state-of-the-art GP-based or deep learning MF regression methods, ranking highest in accuracy and uncertainty quantification with runtime advantages. Limitations include context window constraints and dependence on the quality of the pre-trained TFM's.
item.dc:creator: Rosen Ting-Ying Yu, Nicholas Sung, Faez Ahmed

item.title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2602.00628v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM's hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms -- similarity-based forced choice and free association -- over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306, 2026
item.dc:creator: Louis Schiekiera, Max Zimmer, Christophe Roux, Sebastian Pokutta, Fritz G\"unther

item.title: DCD: Decomposition-based Causal Discovery from Autocorrelated and Non-Stationary Temporal Data
item.description: arXiv:2602.01433v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multivariate time series in domains such as finance, climate science, and healthcare often exhibit long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and short-term fluctuations, complicating causal inference under non-stationarity and autocorrelation. Existing causal discovery methods typically operate on raw observations, making them vulnerable to spurious edges and misattributed temporal dependencies. We introduce a decomposition-based causal discovery framework that separates each time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components and performs component-specific causal analysis. Trend components are assessed using stationarity tests, seasonal components using kernel-based dependence measures, and residual components using constraint-based causal discovery. The resulting component-level graphs are integrated into a unified multi-scale causal structure. This approach isolates long- and short-range causal effects, reduces spurious associations, and improves interpretability. Across extensive synthetic benchmarks and real-world climate data, our framework more accurately recovers ground-truth causal structure than state-of-the-art baselines, particularly under strong non-stationarity and temporal autocorrelation.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Hasan Ferdous, Ian Stockwell, Md Osman Gani

item.title: Towards Optimality in Active Preference Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.01581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) depends on high-quality datasets of human preference labels, which are costly to collect. Although active learning has been studied to improve sample efficiency relative to passive collection, many existing approaches adopt classical experimental design criteria such as G- or D-optimality. These objectives are not tailored to the structure of preference learning, leaving open the design of problem-specific algorithms. In this work, we identify a simple intuition specific to preference learning that calls into question the suitability of these existing design objectives. Motivated by this insight, we propose two active learning algorithms. The first provides the first instance-dependent label complexity guarantee for this setting, and the second is a simple, practical greedy method. We show the optimality of our instance-dependent term up to a constant depending on the logit bound, compared with a lower-bound characteristic. We evaluate our algorithms on real-world preference datasets and synthetic data observing improved sample efficiency compared to existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Yao Zhao, Kwang-Sung Jun

item.title: Distance Marching for Generative Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2602.02928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern generative models based on diffusion or flow matching transport noise toward the data manifold, without representing the data manifold explicitly. We propose Distance Marching that explores an alternative design by explicitly modeling a distance field of the data manifold. A distance field offers a geometric view of generation as a descent process toward the data manifold using only the current position. The negative gradient of the distance field provides the direction, and the distance value can optionally determine the step size. However, sparse training data in high-dimensional space make it difficult to identify the closest points on the data manifold needed to train the distance field. To address this challenge, we design new loss functions that emphasize denoising targets from closer data points. Our analysis shows that, without time input, emphasizing closer targets reduces denoising ambiguity and the bias toward the data mean. This distance-field perspective naturally motivates two principled deterministic samplers, showing fast convergence in inference. As a result, our model is the only one without time input that remains competitive with time-conditioned models across datasets and architectures. Moreover, our distance prediction is also helpful for early stopping during sampling and for out-of-distribution detection. We hope distance-field modeling can open a promising direction for exploring generative modeling from a geometric perspective.
item.dc:creator: Zimo Wang, Ishit Mehta, Haolin Lu, Xunpeng Huang, Chung-En Sun, Ge Yan, Tsui-Wei Weng, Tzu-Mao Li

item.title: Grables: When Graph Structure Helps Tabular Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2602.03945v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simple row-wise predictors that score each row independently remain competitive with far more expressive architectures on tabular benchmarks, which are i.i.d. by construction. They cannot, however, represent natural targets on transactional, temporal, and relational tables, where labels depend on other rows. We show that row-wise prediction provably rules out targets driven by global counts, overlaps, and relational patterns. To make ``using structure'' precise across architectures, we introduce grables: a modular interface that separates how a table is lifted to a graph (constructor) from how predictions are computed on that graph (node predictor), placing gradient-boosted trees, neighbourhood aggregation, transformer-style tabular models, and relational GNNs on a single axis and pinpointing where expressive power comes from. The framework yields a hierarchy that answers when structure is needed: row-local models suffice for extension-invariant targets, lightweight neighbourhood aggregation captures shallow inter-row signals, and explicit graph construction is needed for compositional patterns that fixed aggregations cannot express without exponential feature blow-up. Experiments on synthetic, transactional, and relational data confirm the predicted separations, but also show that benchmark performance is a poor proxy for structural capability: row-local models score well on tasks they provably cannot represent, and a stress-test that suppresses row-local cues is needed to expose the gap. Conversely, access to cross-row context does not imply a model uses it. Feeding explicitly extracted inter-row structure to strong tabular learners yields gains exactly where the hierarchy predicts. The practical recipe is to add structure incrementally, and only where the target is extension-sensitive.
item.dc:creator: Tamara Cucumides, Floris Geerts

item.title: Flow Matching for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Actions
item.description: arXiv:2602.06138v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative policies based on diffusion models and flow matching have shown strong promise for offline reinforcement learning (RL), but their applicability remains largely confined to continuous action spaces. To address a broader range of offline RL settings, we extend flow matching to a general framework that supports discrete action spaces with multiple objectives. Specifically, we replace continuous flows with continuous-time Markov chains, trained using a Q-weighted flow matching objective. We then extend our design to multi-agent settings, mitigating the exponential growth of joint action spaces via a factorized conditional path. We theoretically show that, under idealized conditions, optimizing this objective recovers the optimal policy. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that our method performs robustly across diverse settings and benchmarks, including high-dimensional control, multi-agent games, and dynamically changing preferences over multiple objectives, while outperforming traditional offline RL methods in practical multi-modal decision-making scenarios. Our discrete framework can also be applied to continuous-control problems through action quantization, providing a flexible trade-off between representational complexity and performance.
item.dc:creator: Fairoz Nower Khan, Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Ruiquan Huang, Haibo Yang, Peizhong Ju

item.title: A Behavior-first approach to Multi-Intention Inverse Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.07496v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) seeks to infer reward functions from expert demonstrations. When demonstrations originate from multiple experts with different intentions, the problem is known as Multi-Intention IRL (MI-IRL). Recent deep generative MI-IRL approaches couple behavior clustering and reward learning, but typically require prior knowledge of the number of true behavioral modes $K^*$. This reliance on expert knowledge limits their adaptability to new behaviors, and only enables analysis related to the learned rewards, and not across the behavior modes used to train them. We propose Contrastive Multi-Intention IRL (CoMI-IRL), a transformer-based unsupervised framework that decouples behavior representation and clustering from downstream reward learning. Our experiments show that CoMI-IRL outperforms existing approaches without a priori knowledge of $K^*$ or labels, while allowing for visual interpretation of behavior relationships and adaptation to unseen behavior without full retraining.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2026. ISSN 2835-8856
item.dc:creator: Antonio Mone, Frans A. Oliehoek, Luciano Cavalcante Siebert

item.title: On the Dynamics of Delayed Generalization in Linear Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.08302v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Delayed generalization, where training accuracy becomes nearly perfect substantially before test accuracy, has often been studied in the context of the depth and compositional structure of deep networks. In this paper, we ask whether delayed generalization can occur in simpler settings. We show that it can arise in a linear model trained with gradient descent and an exponential-tail loss on linearly separable data. We characterize the finite-time hyperplane dynamics into three phases: a population phase, a support vector dominated unlearning phase and a generalization phase. The convergence of the residual beyond the maximum-margin direction is sufficient for the unlearning phase to begin. In the support vector dominated phase, we characterize the hyperplane dynamics. The time scale in these dynamics causes delayed generalization. We validate our theory through controlled experiments varying population and support-vector distributions, and further verify the predicted bias behavior in a deep model with a single output neuron on MNIST. Our results provide a unified characterization of the asymptotic and finite-time dynamics underlying delayed generalization in linear models.
item.dc:creator: Atreya Vedantam, Nataraj Das, Chandrashekar Lakshminarayanan

item.title: Certified Per-Instance Unlearning Using Individual Sensitivity Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2602.15602v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Certified machine unlearning can be achieved through noise injection, with differential privacy guarantees obtained by calibrating the noise to worst-case sensitivity. Yet, the influence of individual training points is highly heterogeneous, making such uniform calibration unnecessarily conservative for most deletion requests. We consider certified per-instance unlearning, a data-dependent notion of certified deletion in which the unlearning mechanism and its certificate can adapt to the point being removed. Our framework turns point-specific sensitivity information into formal unlearning guarantees, allowing the amount of noise to reflect the difficulty of the deletion request rather than the worst case. When training is deterministic, we derive explicit per-instance unlearning certificates. For noisy gradient descent, in the case of ridge regression, similar certificates are obtained through high-probability sensitivity bounds. Experiments on NYU-Depth with frozen DINOv2 features show substantial variation in deletion difficulty across points, and demonstrate that per-instance calibration can substantially improve utility over uniform worst-case calibration.
item.dc:creator: Hanna Benarroch (DI-ENS), Jamal Atif (CMAP), Olivier Capp\'e (DI-ENS)

item.title: A Structural Theory of Position Bias in Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2602.16837v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformer models systematically favor certain token positions, yet the architectural origins of this position bias remain poorly understood. This bias is closely connected to the Lost-in-the-Middle phenomenon, where models underutilize information placed in the middle of the context. We show that causal Transformer architectures induce a systematic position-bias prior that can help explain the influence profiles associated with Lost-in-the-Middle. To characterize this prior, we develop a structural theory based on cumulative attention rollout with layerwise residual mixing. At finite depth, we isolate the competing positional drifts induced by causal masking, residual mixing, and positional encoding. Their interaction produces broad, often U-shaped profiles. At infinite depth, prior work predicts inevitable collapse under attention-only theory and identifies the discrepancy with observed Transformer behavior as an open problem. Under the stated boundedness assumptions, our residual-aware analysis replaces inevitable collapse with a dichotomy governed by cumulative attention mixing. Empirically, across 30 model-dataset settings, our adaptive residual-aware rollout closely matches measured input-token influence and reduces the average profile discrepancy by approximately 85% relative to both the attention-only and fixed-residual rollout baselines.
item.dc:creator: Hanna Herasimchyk, Robin Labryga, Tomislav Prusina, S\"oren Laue

item.title: What is the Value of Censored Data? An Exact Analysis for the Data-driven Newsvendor
item.description: arXiv:2602.16842v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the offline data-driven newsvendor problem when historical demand is censored by past inventory levels. We introduce a class of policies for which worst-case expected regret over all bounded demand distributions admits an exact finite-dimensional characterization, valid for any sample size and historical inventory design. The dimension depends on the number of distinct inventory levels, rather than the number of observations. This framework yields exact analyses of the sales-as-demand heuristic, the Kaplan-Meier policy, and recent policies from the censored-newsvendor literature. We leverage this reduction to derive sharp insights on the achievable performance of standard inventory policies under demand censoring. In particular, our analysis of the Kaplan-Meier policy shows that while demand censoring fundamentally limits what can be learned from passive sales data, just a small amount of targeted exploration at high inventory levels can substantially improve worst-case guarantees. Finally, we further leverage our reduction to design new policies that push the frontier and substantially improve upon the worst-case regret of known policies, reducing it by up to 40%.
item.dc:creator: Rachitesh Kumar, Omar Mouchtaki

item.title: Prompt Interference in LLM Post-Training: Why Pass@k Optimization Can Degrade Pass@1
item.description: arXiv:2602.21189v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pass@$k$ is a widely used performance metric for verifiable large language model tasks, including mathematical reasoning, code generation, and short-answer reasoning. It defines success if any of $k$ independently sampled solutions passes a verifier. This multi-sample inference metric has motivated inference-aware fine-tuning methods that directly optimize pass@$k$. However, prior work reports a trade-off: pass@$k$ improves while pass@1 degrades under such methods. This trade-off is practically important because pass@1 often remains a hard operational constraint due to latency and cost budgets, imperfect verifier coverage, and the need for a reliable single-shot fallback. We study the origin of this trade-off and provide a theoretical characterization of when pass@$k$ policy optimization can reduce pass@1 through gradient conflict induced by prompt interference. This interference arises because shared model parameters couple prompts, so improving performance on some prompts can adversely affect others. We show that pass@$k$ policy gradients can conflict with pass@1 gradients because pass@$k$ optimization implicitly reweights prompts toward low-success prompts; when these prompts are negatively interfering, their upweighting can rotate the pass@$k$ update direction away from the pass@1 direction. We illustrate our findings with large language model experiments on verifiable mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.
item.dc:creator: Anas Barakat, Souradip Chakraborty, Khushbu Pahwa, Amrit Singh Bedi

item.title: Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement
item.description: arXiv:2602.22507v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and within-plan public-space advantage (PIA). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback improves IPD and PIA across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyang Jiang, Dongqing Zhang, Qingxiang Liu, Yuxuan Liang

item.title: An Analysis of Role Semantics in Directed Dynamic Graph Modeling for Edge Classification
item.description: arXiv:2602.23135v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Edge classification on directed dynamic graphs is critical for understanding evolving user-item interactions and behavioral patterns in recommender systems and social platforms. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically process these interactions using shared parameters for nodes with semantically distinct roles, including source, destination, query, and neighbor. While abundant supervision in tasks such as link prediction provides sufficient gradient signal for models to implicitly deduce role semantics and overcome this conflation, there are often far fewer labels available for edge classification. We hypothesize that in such regimes, the ability of models to implicitly separate roles is restricted, degrading downstream performance. To empirically investigate this relationship, we introduce an experimental framework for sequence-based models that explicitly disentangles functional roles using targeted embeddings and an asymmetric pretraining objective. By providing architectural priors for these roles, the framework serves as an evaluative vehicle to isolate and measure the resulting performance delta across a range of label budgets. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that this explicit role disentanglement yields substantial and consistent relative performance gains over baselines. Furthermore, representational analyses reveal that the mechanism by which the framework provides these benefits is a bifurcation of source and destination latent spaces that improves linear separability.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Bonnet, Marek Rei

item.title: TopoCurate:Modeling Interaction Topology for Tool-Use Agent Training
item.description: arXiv:2603.01714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training tool-use agents typically relies on outcome-based filtering: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on successful trajectories and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on pass-rate-selected tasks. However, this paradigm ignores interaction dynamics: successful trajectories may lack error recovery or exhibit redundancy, while pass rates fail to distinguish structurally informative tasks from trivial ones. We propose \textbf{TopoCurate}, an interaction-aware framework that projects multi-trial rollouts from the same task into a unified semantic quotient topology. By merging equivalent action-observation states, this projection transforms scattered linear trajectories into a structured manifold that explicitly captures how tool invocations and environmental responses drive the divergence between effective strategies and failure modes. Leveraging this representation, we introduce a dual-selection mechanism: for SFT, we prioritize trajectories demonstrating reflective recovery, semantic efficiency, and strategic diversity to mitigate covariate shift and mode collapse; for RL, we select tasks with high error branch ratios and strategic heterogeneity, maximizing gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio to address vanishing signals in sparse-reward settings. Evaluations on BFCLv3 and Tau2 Bench show that TopoCurate achieves consistent gains of 4.2\% (SFT) and 6.9\% (RL) over state-of-the-art baselines. We will release the code and data soon for further investigations.
item.dc:creator: Jinluan Yang, Yuxin Liu, Zhengyu Chen, Chengcheng Han, Yueqing Sun, Qi Gu, Hui Su, Xunliang Cai, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang

item.title: Learning Shortest Paths with Generative Flow Networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.01786v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we present a novel learning framework for finding shortest paths in graphs utilizing Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). First, we examine theoretical properties of GFlowNets in non-acyclic environments in relation to shortest paths. We prove that, if the total flow is minimized, forward and backward policies traverse the environment graph exclusively along shortest paths between the initial and terminal states. Building on this result, we reduce shortest-path finding in an arbitrary unweighted graph to finding a non-acyclic GFlowNet with minimal total flow, and approximate it in practice by training with flow regularization. We experimentally demonstrate the performance of our method in pathfinding in permutation environments and in solving Rubik's Cubes of various sizes. For the latter problems, our approach shows competitive results with state-of-the-art machine learning approaches designed specifically for this task in terms of the solution length, while requiring smaller search budget at test-time.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Morozov, Ian Maksimov, Daniil Tiapkin, Sergey Samsonov

item.title: Next-token Preference: Scaling Unsupervised Reward Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2603.02225v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning from feedback advances the capabilities and safety of frontier models, but preference supervision remains costly and difficult to scale. We introduce next-token preference (NTP), an unsupervised reward-modeling method that constructs preference pairs from the continuation structure of raw web text. NTP uses each prefix's original continuation as the chosen response and nearby continuations as in-batch negatives, without candidate generation or human or model-generated preference annotations. Training on 11M tokens of math-focused web data yields steady gains on RewardBench and RewardBench 2, with gains across model families and sizes. Across mathematical and general-domain web corpora, our method improves overall RewardBench 2 accuracy by 7.6-8.3 percentage points over initialization under the same token budget. Training on math-focused text yields gains of up to +16.1 on in-domain math subsets and consistent improvements on out-of-domain safety and general subsets. These reward models improve best-of-N selection on math, code, safety, and instruction following, and support math policy optimization competitive with supervised reward models of similar size. NTP also improves the label efficiency of subsequent supervised fine-tuning. Using half the labeled pairs from a curated preference dataset, NTP initialization surpasses base initialization trained on the full dataset. These results suggest that web text contains transferable preference signals that can reduce dependence on costly preference annotations.
item.dc:creator: Jingxuan Fan, Yueying Li, Zhenting Qi, Dinghuai Zhang, Kiant\'e Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang

item.title: Less Noise, Same Certificate: Retain Sensitivity for Unlearning
item.description: arXiv:2603.03172v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Certified machine unlearning aims to provably remove the influence of a deletion set $U$ from a model trained on a dataset $S$, by producing an unlearned output that is statistically indistinguishable from retraining on the retain set $R := S\setminus U$. Many existing certified unlearning methods adapt techniques from Differential Privacy (DP) and add noise calibrated to global sensitivity, i.e., the worst-case output change over all adjacent datasets. We show that this DP-style calibration is often overly conservative: unlike DP, unlearning requires no indistinguishability across different retain sets, only between each deletion output and retraining on the same retain set $R$. Motivated by this distinction, we define retain sensitivity as the worst-case output change over deletions $U'$ from $R\cup U'$ while keeping $R$ fixed. While insufficient for DP, retain sensitivity is exactly sufficient for unlearning, allowing for the same certificates with less noise. We validate these reductions in noise theoretically and empirically across several problems, including the weight of minimum spanning trees, PCA, and ERM. Finally, we refine the analysis of two widely used certified unlearning algorithms through the lens of retain sensitivity, leveraging the regularity induced by $R$ to further reduce noise and improve utility.
item.dc:creator: Carolin Heinzler, Kasra Malihi, Amartya Sanyal

item.title: SERQ: Saliency-Aware Low-Rank Error Reconstruction for LLM Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2603.08185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a prevailing technique for deploying large language models (LLMs) efficiently in terms of both memory and computation, across edge devices and server platforms. Existing PTQ methods primarily aim to reduce precision in weights and activations by mitigating quantization errors caused by channel-wise outlier activations (e.g., pre-quantization scaling, online transformations, or low-rank error reconstruction). Among these approaches, error reconstruction with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has proven particularly effective, as it introduces a lightweight auxiliary computation path without requiring heavy optimization or additional online layers. However, prior studies reveal severe accuracy degradation under W4A4 settings, and conventional low-rank adaptations rely on two sequential factors, necessitating intermediate quantization during inference and thereby limiting low-precision efficiency. In this work, we propose SERQ, a saliency-aware error reconstruction method for low-bit LLM inference that employs a single low-rank compensation matrix. SERQ preserves efficient 4-bit matrix multiplication in linear layers by jointly mitigating quantization errors arising from both activation and weight saliency through three stages: (1) static activation flattening, (2) saliency-aware error reconstruction, and (3) offline weight permutation. The method incurs additional computation only for low-rank error reconstruction via a single decomposition, while all other operations are performed offline, thereby keeping latency overhead minimal. Empirically, SERQ outperforms prior error reconstruction methods under both W4A8 and W4A4 settings, and achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art rotation-based W4A4 approaches, while substantially reducing calibration complexity. Code is available at https://github.com/acalabys/SERQ
item.dc:creator: Yeonsik Park, Hyeonseong Kim, Seungkyu Choi

item.title: Grammar of the Wave: Towards Explainable Multivariate Time Series Event Detection via Neuro-Symbolic VLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.11479v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time Series Event Detection (TSED) aims to localize semantically meaningful events in time series data, with critical applications in high-stakes domains. Unlike statistical anomalies, events are often defined by natural-language descriptions with internal temporal-logic structures across multiple physical channels. However, in real-world settings, dense event annotations are expensive to obtain, making purely supervised learning difficult. We introduce Language-guided TSED, a setting where a model is given textual event descriptions and must ground them to intervals in multivariate signals with little or no labeled data. To address this problem, we propose Event Logic Tree (ELT), a knowledge representation framework that converts linguistic descriptions into structured temporal logic over signal primitives. Building on ELT, we present SELA, a neuro-symbolic VLM agent framework that iteratively grounds primitives from signal visualizations and composes them under ELT constraints, producing both event intervals and faithful tree-structured explanations. We further release a real-world benchmark across energy and climate domains with expert knowledge and annotations. Experiments show that SELA improves over supervised fine-tuning and existing zero/few-shot time series reasoning baselines.
item.dc:creator: Sky Chenwei Wan, Yifei Y. Wang, Tianjun Hou, Xiqing Chang, Aymeric Jan

item.title: Deep probabilistic model synthesis enables unified modeling of whole-brain neural activity across individual subjects
item.description: arXiv:2603.14161v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many disciplines need quantitative models that synthesize experimental data across multiple instances of the same general system. For example, neuroscientists must combine data from the brains of many individual animals to understand the species' brain in general. However, typical machine learning models treat one system instance at a time. Here we introduce a machine learning framework, deep probabilistic model synthesis (DPMS), that leverages system properties auxiliary to the model to combine data across system instances. DPMS specifically uses variational inference to learn a conditional prior distribution and instance-specific posterior distributions over model parameters that respectively tie together the system instances and capture their unique structure. DPMS can synthesize a wide variety of model classes, such as those for regression, classification, and dimensionality reduction, and we demonstrate its ability to improve upon single-instance models on synthetic data and whole-brain neural activity data from larval zebrafish.
item.dc:creator: William E. Bishop, Luuk W. Hesselink, Bernhard Englitz, Misha B. Ahrens, James E. Fitzgerald

item.title: DyJR: Preserving Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Dynamic Jensen-Shannon Replay
item.description: arXiv:2603.16157v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While Reinforcement Learning (RL) enhances Large Language Model reasoning, on-policy algorithms like GRPO are sample-inefficient as they discard past rollouts. Existing experience replay methods address this by reusing accurate samples for direct policy updates, but this can incur additional storage costs and concentrate the policy on a narrow set of solutions. We argue that historical data should prioritize sustaining local policy plasticity rather than simply reinforcing accuracy. We define local policy plasticity as a persistent ability to remain backtrackable and switchable with respect to recent successful trajectories: throughout training, the policy maintains non-negligible support on recently reachable alternatives, so it can smoothly reallocate probability mass when needed without being locked into a single dominant path. To this end, we propose Dynamic Jensen-Shannon Replay (DyJR), a simple yet effective regularization framework using a dynamic reference distribution from recent trajectories. DyJR introduces two innovations: (1) A Time-Sensitive Dynamic Buffer that uses FIFO and adaptive sizing to retain only temporally proximal samples, synchronizing with model evolution; and (2) Jensen-Shannon Divergence Regularization, which replaces direct replay policy-gradient updates with a regularization signal that discourages premature over-commitment to a single Rank-1 trajectory. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, Text-to-SQL, and coding benchmarks demonstrate that DyJR improves over GRPO as well as baselines such as RLEP and Ex-GRPO, while maintaining training efficiency comparable to the original GRPO. Furthermore, Rank-k token probability evolution and semantic-mode analyses show reduced concentration and greater retention of alternative continuations. Matched admission-objective comparisons and repeated runs provide additional evidence for the roles of DyJR's components.
item.dc:creator: Long Li, Zhijian Zhou, Tianyi Wang, Weidi Xu, Zuming Huang, Wei Chu, Zhe Wang, Shirui Pan, Chao Qu, Yuan Qi

item.title: Holistic Scaling Laws for Optimal Mixture-of-Experts Architecture Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2603.21862v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling laws govern macroscopic resource allocation for LLMs, yet precise architectural configurations for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain guided by heuristics. Existing MoE scaling studies either incorporate MoE-specific variables into scaling formulas, causing fitted coefficients to grow rapidly without proportional experimental support, or fix all non-MoE factors, implicitly assuming global architecture does not influence local MoE scaling. We propose a reusable framework for holistic MoE architectural optimization. We first show that MoE architectures decouple FLOPs per token ($M$), active parameters ($N_a$), and total parameters ($N$), which serve as distinct proxies for computation, weight access, and parameter storage. We therefore establish a joint constraint triad of $M$, active parameters ($N_a$), and total parameters ($N$) for rigorous MoE characterization. To tame the resulting $O(n^{16})$ search space, we employ mathematical decoupling: structural constraints and a rank-preserving property of the hidden dimension factorize the optimization into an $O(n^3) + O(n^2)$ two-phase search. Through extensive validation across 670+ MoE models spanning $10^{18}$ to $3 \times 10^{20}$ FLOPs, we derive globally applicable scaling laws mapping any compute budget to its optimal architecture. A key finding is that the near-optimal configuration band widens with scale, providing a quantitative basis for trade-offs between scaling law recommendations and engineering constraints. Our work delivers actionable blueprints for optimal MoE design under arbitrary compute budgets.
item.dc:creator: Weilin Wan, Jingtao Han, Debing Zhang, Weizhong Zhang, Cheng Jin

item.title: Structural Pass Analysis in Football: Learning Pass Archetypes and Tactical Impact from Spatio-Temporal Tracking Data
item.description: arXiv:2603.28916v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Passing actions are commonly evaluated through ball progression and attacking outcomes, yet their relationship with the spatial organisation of the opposition provides an additional perspective on passing behaviour. This study introduces an interpretable framework for describing passing structure using synchronised event and tracking data. Three complementary descriptors are proposed: Line Bypass Score (LBS), measuring the difference in goal-side opponent counts between passer and receiver; Space Gain Metric (SGM), comparing their nearest-opponent distances; and Structural Disruption Index (SDI), summarising differences in defensive organisation between pass initiation and a sampled state one second later. Following transformation and standardisation, these descriptors are combined into Tactical Impact Value (TIV), a fixed-weight structural composite. Applied to 41,078 open-play passing events from the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the framework identifies four interpretable profiles: Circulatory, Destabilising, Line-breaking, and Space-expanding. The profiles exhibit distinct structural signatures and different distributions of territorial-crossing and recorded attacking indicators. Team, spatial, player, and passer--receiver analyses further demonstrate how the representation can describe passing behaviour across analytical scales. The framework complements outcome-oriented approaches by connecting individual passing actions with measurable characteristics of opposition positioning and defensive organisation.
item.dc:creator: Oktay Karaku\c{s}, Hasan Arkada\c{s}, Can Ey\"{u}po\u{g}lu

item.title: Soft MPCritic: Value-Based Reinforcement Learning for Non-Differentiable Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2604.01477v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) and model predictive control (MPC) offer complementary strengths, yet existing MPC-RL frameworks commonly rely on gradient-based optimization and therefore cannot handle the non-differentiable dynamics and objectives common in RL. We propose Soft MPCritic, an MPC-RL framework that learns a soft value function and uses sampling-based planning both for online control and for generating value targets. Specifically, Soft MPCritic instantiates MPC with model predictive path integral control (MPPI) and learns a terminal Q-function through fitted value iteration. Because the value targets are computed by the same planner used for control, the learned value function is aligned with the planner and implicitly extends its effective horizon. To keep target generation tractable, we introduce an amortized warm-start strategy that reuses the open-loop action sequences planned during online control to initialize batched MPPI computations of value targets, reducing computational cost without sacrificing solution quality. For robustness to model error, Soft MPCritic plans over scenarios drawn from an ensemble of dynamics models trained for next-step prediction. On both classical and constrained control tasks, Soft MPCritic learns effective policies with non-differentiable objectives, particularly where finite-horizon MPPI alone falls short. Soft MPCritic thus offers a practical blueprint for synthesizing MPC policies directly from black-box objectives, without differentiable surrogates.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Banker, Nathan P. Lawrence, Ali Mesbah

item.title: Process Rewards for Outcome-Guided Reasoning Steps in LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.02341v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models has improved substantially with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards, where final answers can be checked automatically and converted into reliable training signals. Most such pipelines optimize outcome correctness only, which yields sparse feedback for long, multi-step solutions and offers limited guidance on intermediate reasoning errors. Recent work therefore introduces process reward models (PRMs) to score intermediate steps and provide denser supervision. In practice, PRM scores are often imperfectly aligned with final correctness and can reward locally fluent reasoning that still ends in an incorrect answer. When optimized as absolute rewards, such signals can amplify fluent failure modes and induce reward hacking. We propose PROGRS, a framework that leverages PRMs while keeping outcome correctness dominant. PROGRS treats process rewards as relative preferences within outcome groups rather than absolute targets. We introduce outcome-conditioned centering, which shifts PRM scores of incorrect trajectories to have zero mean within each prompt group. It removes systematic bias while preserving informative rankings. PROGRS combines a frozen quantile-regression PRM with a multi-scale coherence evaluator. We integrate the resulting centered process bonus into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) without auxiliary objectives or additional trainable components. Across MATH-500, AMC, AIME, MinervaMath, and OlympiadBench, PROGRS consistently improves Pass@1 over outcome-only baselines and achieves stronger performance with fewer rollouts. These results show that outcome-conditioned centering enables safe and effective use of process rewards for mathematical reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Rezaei, Jens Lehmann, Sahar Vahdati

item.title: Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models
item.description: arXiv:2604.03208v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models are a promising path to zero-shot embodied control through planning. However, existing world model planners struggle on long-horizon, multi-stage tasks: prediction errors compound and naive search is exponential in the planning horizon. Hierarchy mitigates both by decomposing tasks into shorter, tractable subproblems; yet prior hierarchical approaches either amortize control into task-specific policies (hierarchical RL) or assume low-dimensional states and known dynamics (classical hierarchical MPC). We present Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models (HWM), an architecture and planning paradigm for hierarchical model predictive control directly on visual world models trained solely via next-latent prediction. HWM learns world models at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, so predictions from the long horizon model serve as subgoals for the short horizon model via latent matching, without task-specific rewards or hierarchical policies. To keep long-horizon search tractable, HWM learns an action encoder that compresses primitive action chunks into latent macro-actions. On real-world Franka manipulation, HWM solves pick-and-place from a single goal image at 70% success vs. 0% for single-level planning. Across simulated push manipulation and maze navigation, HWM consistently improves performance on long-horizon tasks while requiring up to 3x less planning compute.
item.dc:creator: Wancong Zhang, Basile Terver, Artem Zholus, Soham Chitnis, Harsh Sutaria, Mido Assran, Randall Balestriero, Amir Bar, Yann LeCun, Nicolas Ballas

item.title: The causal relation between off-street parking and electric vehicle adoption in Scotland
item.description: arXiv:2604.09271v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The transition to electric mobility hinges on maximising aggregate adoption while also facilitating equitable access. This study examines whether the 'charging divide' between households with and without off-street parking reflects a genuine infrastructure constraint or a by-product of socio-economic disparity. Moving beyond conventional predictive models, we apply a probabilistic causal framework to a nationally representative dataset of Scottish households, enabling estimation of policy interventions while explicitly neutralising the confounding effect of other causal factors. The results reveal a structural hierarchy in the EV adoption process. Private off-street parking functions as a conversion catalyst: enabling access to home-charging increases the probability of EV ownership from 3.3% to 5.6% (a 70% relative, 2.3 percentage point absolute increase). However, this effect primarily accelerates households already economically positioned to purchase an EV rather than recruiting new entrants. By contrast, household income operates as the fundamental affordability ceiling. A causal contrast between lower- and higher-income strata, shows a reduction in market non-participation by 23.1 percentage points, identifying financial capacity as the principal gatekeeper to entering the EV transition funnel. Crucially, the analysis demonstrates that standard observational models overstate the isolated effect of off-street parking infrastructure. The apparent effect emerges from selection bias: higher-income households are disproportionately likely to possess both private parking and the means to purchase EVs. These findings support a dual-track policy strategy: lowering the affordability ceiling for non-participants through financial instruments, while addressing EV home-charging access for the 'latent intent' cohort in high-density urban contexts.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: D'Amico, Bernardino, Achille Fonzone, and Emma Hart. "The causal relation between off-street parking and electric vehicle adoption in Scotland. "Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice", 214 (2026): 105294
item.dc:creator: Bernardino D'Amico, Achille Fonzone, Emma Hart

item.title: Learning to Test: Latent Representation Learning for Dynamic Instability Detection
item.description: arXiv:2604.10967v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stability assessment is central to safety-critical systems governed by differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), whose dynamics are constrained by physical laws and admissibility conditions. These systems operate under stochastically varying environmental inputs, so stability must be reassessed as the context distribution shifts, yet repeated large-scale DAE simulation is prohibitive in high-dimensional or real-time settings. We propose a test-oriented learning framework that tests a trajectory-level chance constraint from deployment contexts alone. Rather than re-estimating physical parameters or re-solving the DAE, we learn a latent representation from baseline context-trajectory data that retains stability-relevant information and is regularized toward a tractable reference distribution, and calibrate a latent discrepancy test over the composite safety null. We establish exact validity for oracle calibration and asymptotic validity for its empirical implementation under class-conditional latent invariance, and show that the guarantee degrades gracefully when this invariance holds only approximately. On simulated dynamical systems and a power-system real-world example, our approach strikes a balance between validity and power, whereas other baseline methods each fail in at least one regime. An ablation that injects controlled violations of the invariance assumption shows that decisions stay correct while the violation is below the safety margin, as the theory predicts.
item.dc:creator: Minxing Zheng, Zewei Deng, Liyan Xie, Shixiang Zhu

item.title: Beyond Single-Model Optimization: Preserving Plasticity in Continual Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.15414v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning must balance retention with adaptation, yet many methods still rely on \emph{single-model preservation}, committing to one evolving policy as the main reusable solution across tasks. Even when a previously successful policy is retained, it may no longer provide a reliable starting point for rapid adaptation after interference, reflecting a form of \emph{loss of plasticity} that single-policy preservation cannot address. Inspired by quality-diversity methods, we introduce \textsc{TeLAPA} (Transfer-Enabled Latent-Aligned Policy Archives), a continual RL framework that organizes behaviorally diverse policy neighborhoods into per-task archives and maintains a shared latent space so that archived policies remain comparable and reusable under non-stationary drift. This perspective shifts continual RL from retaining isolated solutions to maintaining \emph{skill-aligned neighborhoods} with competent and behaviorally related policies that support future relearning. In our MiniGrid CL setting, \textsc{TeLAPA} learns more tasks successfully, recovers competence faster on revisited tasks after interference, and retains higher performance across a sequence of tasks. Our analyses show that source-optimal policies are often not transfer-optimal, even within a local competent neighborhood, and that effective reuse depends on retaining and selecting among multiple nearby alternatives rather than collapsing them to one representative. Together, these results reframe continual RL around reusable and competent policy neighborhoods, providing a route beyond single-model preservation toward more plastic lifelong agents.
item.dc:creator: Lute Lillo, Nick Cheney

item.title: L1 Regularization Paths in Linear Models by Parametric Gaussian Message Passing
item.description: arXiv:2604.16949v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper proposes new algorithms for computing the regularization path of linear-model fitting (i) with L1 costs for the independent variables and L2 costs for the dependent variables, and (ii) with L2 costs for the independent variables and L1 costs for the dependent variables. Unlike previously proposed algorithms, the proposed algorithms for (i) and (ii) are exact duals of each other. The heart of the proposed algorithms is parametric Gaussian message passing (i.e., Kalman-type forward-backward recursions) in the pertinent factor graphs. We first develop such algorithms for linear models with general (but preferably low-dimensional) state space representations. We then specialize to specific state space representations of generic linear models; in this case, the structure of the factor graph allows to refine the proposed algorithms such that the computational complexity drops to linear scale.
item.dc:creator: Yun-Peng Li, Hans-Andrea Loeliger

item.title: Cover meets Robbins while Betting on Bounded Data: $\ln n$ Regret and Almost Sure $\ln\ln n$ Regret
item.description: arXiv:2604.20172v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consider betting against a sequence of $[0,1]$-valued observations using bets that are fair if the data have a conditional mean $m_0 \in (0,1)$. Cover's universal portfolio algorithm achieves a worst-case regret of $O(\ln n)$ compared to the best constant bet in hindsight, and this logarithmic order is unimprovable against adversarial data. We construct an explicit full-support Robbins mixture that combines insights from Robbins and Cover. It retains $O(\ln n)$ regret on every path while also eventually satisfying $R_n\le(1+o(1))\ln\ln V_n$ on every path with bounded mixture wealth and $V_n\to\infty$, where $V_n$ is an intrinsic variance process. It also attains the optimal asymptotic wealth growth rate under iid alternatives. Under the conditional-mean claim and almost-sure divergence of $V_n$, the sharper regret bound holds almost surely, and its leading constant $1$ is unimprovable. We also give explicit finite-time, path-wise regret bounds. A simple hedging principle shows how splitting initial wealth between two strategies achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee by retaining the smaller of their regrets and the larger of their growth rates. We contrast our results to those for unbounded data in Agrawal and Ramdas (2026). Their worst-case regret is unbounded. However, hedging yields almost-sure iterated-logarithmic regret together with optimal growth. Finally, our wealth process witnesses a sharp game-theoretic upper law of iterated logarithm, analogous to Shafer and Vovk (2005).
item.dc:creator: Shubhada Agrawal, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: PermaFrost-Attack: Stealth Pretraining Seeding(SPS) for planting Logic Landmines During LLM Training
item.description: arXiv:2604.22117v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulation, and their reliance on web-scale pretraining creates a subtle but consequential attack surface. We study Stealth Pretraining Seeding (SPS), a threat model in which adversaries distribute small amounts of poisoned content across stealth websites, increasing the likelihood that such material is absorbed into future training corpora derived from sources such as Common Crawl. Because each individual payload is tiny, diffuse, and superficially benign, the attack is difficult to detect during dataset construction or filtering. The result is a latent form of poisoning that remains largely invisible under standard evaluation, yet can later be activated by a precise trigger such as <00TRIGGER00>. We call this attack PermaFrost, reflecting its latent and reactivatable nature. We study it through PermaFrost-Attack, a controlled framework for latent conceptual poisoning, together with three geometric diagnostics: Thermodynamic Length, Spectral Curvature, and the Infection Traceback Graph. Across multiple model families and scales, we show that this controlled SPS proxy can induce persistent unsafe behavior that often remains hidden under standard evaluation. Our results identify SPS as a practical and underappreciated threat to future foundation models. This paper introduces a novel geometric diagnostic lens for systematically examining latent model behavior, providing a principled foundation for detecting, characterizing, and understanding vulnerabilities that may remain invisible under standard evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Harsh Kumar, Rahul Maity, Tanmay Joshi, Aman Chadha, Vinija Jain, Suranjana Trivedy, Amitava Das

item.title: Probabilistic Circuits for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2604.27814v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint probabilistic modeling is essential for forecasting irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) to accurately quantify uncertainty. Existing approaches often struggle to balance model expressivity with consistent marginalization, frequently leading to unreliable or contradictory forecasts. To address this, we propose CircuITS, a novel architecture for probabilistic IMTS forecasting based on sum-product networks (SPNs). Our model is flexible in capturing intricate dependencies between time series channels while structurally guaranteeing valid joint distributions. Experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that CircuITS achieves superior joint and marginal density estimation compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
item.dc:creator: Christian Kl\"otergens, Lars Schmidt-Thieme, Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi

item.title: AdNGCL: Adaptive Negative Scheduling for Graph Contrastive Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.03076v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Negative samples play a crucial role in graph contrastive learning (GCL), yet existing methods mainly focus on which negatives should be selected, mined, filtered, or progressively introduced. Less attention has been given to separating the negative candidates available to an anchor from the subset that actively participates in optimization, and to adapting this exposure according to training behavior. To address this gap, we propose the Adaptive Negative Scheduling for Graph Contrastive Learning (AdNGCL) framework, which maintains a bounded per-anchor candidate reservoir and periodically reassesses candidate hardness as representations evolve. Its core component, Hardness-Aware Negative Scheduling (HANS), uses a category-specific training-response signal to determine whether exposure to easy, intermediate, or hard negatives should increase at each scheduling opportunity. Furthermore, reliability-aware candidate refresh handles potentially positive-like candidates, while within-category diversity refresh changes active identities without altering HANS-controlled exposure. AdNGCL retains a standard symmetric InfoNCE objective. Experiments on ten benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art self-supervised graph learning methods show that AdNGCL achieves the highest mean Micro-F1 among the evaluated methods on eight datasets, with improvements of up to 1.30 percentage points over the second-best method, ranks second on Actor, and remains competitive on Coauthor-CS. Ablation, sensitivity, scheduler and reliability diagnostics, and computational analyses further examine the behavior and contribution of the proposed mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Adnan Ali, Jinlong Li, Syed Muhammad Israr, Guanghua Yang, Ali Kashif Bashir, Mohammed Ameen

item.title: Bilinear Mamba-Koopman Neural MPC for Varying Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2605.04793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Koopman-based neural MPC models generate time-varying dynamics from historical data, but preserve convexity by enforcing that the system operator is independent of the current control input. This conditional independence constraint limits adaptation to changing dynamics within a single MPC horizon, particularly under time-varying conditions and under stale-plan execution. We propose Bilinear Mamba-Koopman Neural MPC, a minimal extension that introduces control-dependent coupling in the latent dynamics, allowing the effective operator to adapt to the current input. The resulting model is a strict generalization of the standard linear, conditional-independence formulation, adds less than 1% parameters through a low-rank structure, and admits exact model Jacobians that enable efficient Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) with monotone-descent and KKT convergence results under standard trust-region assumptions. Across CartPole and RSCP benchmarks in time-invariant and time-varying regimes, the proposed model matches or improves forecasting accuracy on every cell when training noise is averaged out, with strict gains where control-state coupling is structurally present. Its main closed-loop gains appear in the RSCP TV task, where iterative SCP improves adaptation within the horizon and substantially stabilizes training; in CartPole TV, the gains are modest but consistent. In delayed re-planning experiments on the time-varying variants, the bilinear model degrades more gracefully under stale-plan execution, maintaining a consistent advantage on CartPole TV and a substantially larger robustness margin on RSCP TV. These results show that control-dependent latent dynamics provide a simple and effective mechanism for robust MPC under varying conditions.
item.dc:creator: Matan Pagi, Zohar Sorek

item.title: Fitted Q-Iteration with Continuous Actions and Adaptive Data: Smoothed Coverage and Minimax Rates
item.description: arXiv:2605.05791v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fitted Q-iteration (FQI) is well understood when the data come from a fixed distribution and the action set is finite, whereas value-based continuous control collects its data adaptively and maximizes over continuous actions. Both features break the standard analysis: the regression data are dependent, and every density-ratio concentrability coefficient of a deterministic greedy policy is infinite when the exploration has no atoms. Conditioning on the history freezes the regression target, so each round of FQI is a regression with martingale noise, and we obtain localized rates that are fast for classes of polylogarithmic metric entropy. We transfer the regression error to the loss of the greedy policy by smoothing the measures on which this loss is evaluated, at a price that depends on the action dimension and the smoothness of the residuals in the action. Under deterministic dynamics the state is smoothed as well, and the state dimension enters the price. Minimax lower bounds with the same exponents in the sample size show that no learner avoids these prices, for restart data in the case of the state dimension. The coverage conditions do not involve the unknown greedy policies; they hold under exploration floors with restarts and, for action smoothing, bounded transition densities.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Hau{\ss}mann, Mustafa Mert \c{C}elikok, Melih Kandemir

item.title: Selective Successor Eligibility Traces for RLVR
item.description: arXiv:2605.05965v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a key approach for improving the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, widely used critic-free algorithms such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) suffer from coarse-grained temporal credit assignment, as they assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all tokens and fail to distinguish the contributions of different reasoning steps. To address this challenge, we propose Selective Successor Eligibility Traces (S-trace), an critic-free eligibility trace method that enables more effective credit assignment. S-trace introduces successor importance reweighting to recover downstream credit signals under PPO-style clipping and propagates them to selected historical tokens through entropy-based token selection. Theoretically, we establish an upper bound on its discrepancy from the raw eligibility traces-based policy gradient estimator, jointly controlled by the KL divergence and the trace decay factor $\lambda$. Experiments show that S-trace achieves absolute gains in average pass@16 of 1.80\% and 6.17\% over GRPO, and 2.32\% and 0.87\% over trace-style GRPO($\lambda$), on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, respectively, while maintaining robust gains on Qwen3-8B and producing shorter responses.
item.dc:creator: Chaoli Mou, Xinning Chen, Zhan Zhuang, Qinghe Zheng, Deyuan Kong, Yu Zhang

item.title: Requests of a Feather Must Flock Together: Batch Size vs. Prefix Homogeneity in LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2605.06046v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Auto-regressive token generation in large language models is memory-bound because it requires "attending to" key and value tensors (KV cache) of all previous tokens. Prior work aims to improve the efficiency of this decode process by batching multiple requests together, and maximizing batch size subject to GPU memory constraints. The key observation of our work is that with prefix-sharing workloads, smaller, prefix-homogeneous batches - where all requests share a common prefix - can achieve higher decode throughput than larger, heterogeneous batches, due to better spatial and temporal locality during KV cache accesses. However, prefix-aware schedulers in state-of-the-art inference engines maximize prefix reuse within a batch only to reduce KV cache memory footprint, but do not stop batch formation at smaller homogeneous batches that could have performed better. Further, we show that shared prefix detection in existing schedulers relies on radix-tree traversals, incurring substantial CPU overhead that is often comparable to GPU execution time. This paper presents Feather, a prefix-aware scheduler that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn the optimal tradeoff between batch size and prefix homogeneity. We also introduce Chunked Hash Tree (CHT), a lightweight data structure that enables fast prefix detection and efficient request selection for the RL scheduler, avoiding expensive tree traversals. We integrate Feather into vLLM and SGLang, and our evaluation shows that Feather achieves 2-10X higher end-to-end throughput as compared to existing schedulers, while doing no worse than the status quo when the workload does not have enough prefix sharing. Feather achieves these gains by reducing the total number of KV cache accesses, surpassing the performance of prefix-aware attention kernels that have the same goal.
item.dc:creator: Saksham Rathi, Preeti, Mythili Vutukuru

item.title: AdaGamma: State-Dependent Discounting for Temporal Adaptation in Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.06149v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The discount factor in reinforcement learning controls both the effective planning horizon and the strength of bootstrapping, yet most deep RL methods use a single fixed value across all states.
